agree.reason: Dana would likely see the email as relevant because it opens with her own $600,000 quote and says the WMS stays in place, but it never shows her the payback, so a busy VP has little reason to act on it.

honest.reason: Every number is accurate and 'more than half' holds (4.1 to 1.9 is a 54% drop), but the email shows only the best result and leaves out the 2.8-to-2.2 customer, so a single case reads as typical.

works_the_facts.reason: The $75,000 annual total is correctly derived, but the email never sets it against the roughly $300,000 a year that halving her $600,000 in returns could save, which is the strongest true figure available.

right_comparison.reason: Doing nothing means about $600,000 a year in returns keeps coming, but the email names that cost only as a hook and never compares it with the price.

qualification.reason: A result from one customer needs a hedge, but the only one offered is the vague 'whether the numbers could work for you,' with no range, no second data point and nothing she can check.

objections.reason: 'Sits on top of it' partly answers the IT director's likely objection, but the email doesn't say how much IT work or integration is needed, which is what he would ask.

fit.reason: It is short, readable on a phone, ends with one clear ask and is built around the 'cut errors in half' claim the brief wanted.
